question.text: Fund CAS, a Category III AIF pursuing Convertible Arbitrage, takes a long position in Company A's 12% convertible bond and a simultaneous short position in Company A's equity shares. If Company A's equity price RISES significantly above the conversion price, the fund will typically:

answer.text: Hold the bond to maturity and let the short position compound losses indefinitely
Convert the bonds into equity and deliver those shares to cover the short, offsetting the short-side loss
Close both legs at a loss because the arbitrage has broken down permanently
Roll the bond forward and double the short position to restore the hedge

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 11.2.3 (Convertible Arbitrage Strategy), if equity price rises the fund converts the convertible security into equity shares at the fixed conversion ratio and uses those shares to cover the short, compensating for the mark-to-market loss on the short position. Example 11.6 shows a 27.5% ROI via this mechanism. The Trap: Option A ignores the conversion option that is the whole point of the strategy. Option C misreads a successful outcome as failure. Option D adds risk rather than using the embedded conversion option. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-B covers convertible arb at product level; XIX-C tests the Manager's operational execution — the conversion decision is the hedge, not an additional trade. Manager's Pro-Tip: Model the conversion ratio stress-test quarterly — if the company's equity drops 40%+, dividends may be passed and borrowing fees on short leg can exceed coupon income. Set a stop-loss on the convertible leg tied to distance-to-conversion.
